title: Home-made instruments: high and low sounds, and keeping a steady beat

summary.text: Tap a big carton and it booms. Tap a matchbox and it ticks. Both are made of card, so why do they sound so different? When you tap a box, its sides vibrate: they move in and out very fast. A big side vibrates more slowly, and slow vibrations make low sounds. In this unit you make instruments from boxes, bottles and rubber bands, and you test which ones sound high and which sound low. You also learn to keep a beat, a steady pulse like a clock ticking, and to clap a rhythm on top of it. When everyone follows one beat, all the different sounds fit together into music.
summary.art: A child on a floor mat playing a big cardboard carton like a drum, with a little brother shaking a plastic bottle of rice and a grandmother clapping the beat, and a tissue box with a rubber band stretched over it nearby.

intro.hook: Find an empty matchbox and a big empty carton. Tap the middle of each one with one finger. Listen. Both are made of card. So why does one tick and the other boom?
intro.text: In this unit you find out. You make a drum from a box, a hooter from a bottle and a one-string instrument from a rubber band. You test big and small boxes to see which sounds high and which sounds low. Then you learn to keep a steady beat, like drummers all over India do, so that a whole family band can play together.
intro.art: A child's finger tapping a tiny matchbox on one side of the picture, and the same child's palm slapping a big delivery carton on the other, with small quick lines from the matchbox and big slow lines from the carton.

outcomes: I can make an instrument from a box, a bottle or a rubber band, and show which part vibrates to make the sound.
I can sort sounds into high and low, and say that fast vibrations make high sounds and slow vibrations make low ones.
I can test boxes of different sizes fairly, and say that a bigger box of the same material makes a lower sound.
I can keep a steady beat with claps or pats, and clap a rhythm, like the rhythm of my name, on top of it.
I can count one cycle of Adi talam, 8 beats, with claps, finger counts and waves.
I can name other animals that move in time to a beat, and say what scientists still argue about.

terms.meaning: To vibrate means to move to and fro very fast, again and again. Every sound starts with something vibrating.
terms.example: Pluck a stretched rubber band. It goes blurry because it is vibrating.
terms.art: A stretched rubber band drawn blurry in the middle, with small curved lines showing it moving to and fro.

terms.meaning: A musical instrument is something made to vibrate on purpose, so that it makes sounds for music.
terms.example: A veena, a tabla, a flute, and a box drum you make yourself are all instruments.
terms.art: A veena, a tabla, a bamboo flute and a cardboard box drum in a row.

terms.meaning: Pitch is how high or low a sound is. Fast vibrations make a high pitch. Slow vibrations make a low pitch.
terms.example: A mouse's squeak has a high pitch. A big drum's boom has a low pitch.
terms.art: A ladder with a mouse at the top for a high sound and a big drum at the bottom for a low sound.

terms.meaning: A high sound is thin and sharp, like a squeak or a whistle. It comes from fast vibrations.
terms.example: A small steel bowl tapped with a spoon gives a high 'ting'.
terms.art: A small steel bowl being tapped with a spoon, with short quick lines above it.

terms.meaning: A low sound is deep, like a boom or a rumble. It comes from slow vibrations.
terms.example: A big delivery carton slapped with a palm gives a low 'dhum'.
terms.art: A palm slapping a big carton, with long slow wavy lines above it.

terms.meaning: A beat is a steady pulse that repeats, with the same gap each time, like a clock ticking.
terms.example: When you march round the room, your steps make a beat: left, right, left, right.
terms.art: A child marching, with footprints evenly spaced on the floor.

terms.meaning: A rhythm is a pattern of sounds and gaps, some short and some long, that fits over the beat.
terms.example: Clap your name. 'Mee-nak-shi' is a rhythm of three claps.
terms.art: A girl clapping, with three dots in a row above her hands for 'Mee-nak-shi'.

terms.meaning: Tempo is how fast the beat goes. A fast tempo has many beats in a short time. A slow tempo has few.
terms.example: A lullaby has a slow tempo. A dance song has a fast tempo.
terms.art: A mother rocking a baby slowly on one side, and children dancing fast on the other.

terms.meaning: In Indian classical music, a tala is a cycle of beats that repeats again and again. Musicians count it with claps, finger counts and waves of the hand.
terms.example: Adi talam, used in many Carnatic songs, has 8 beats in each cycle.
terms.art: A hand clapping, then fingers being counted, then the hand waving, with the numbers 1 to 8 in a circle.

terms.meaning: A pattern is something that repeats in the same order. A rhythm pattern repeats its sounds in the same order.
terms.example: Clap, clap, pat. Clap, clap, pat. Clap, clap, pat.
terms.art: A row of hands: two clapping hands and one hand patting a knee, repeated three times.

explanations.context: This card is about how home-made instruments make their sounds.
explanations.definition: A musical instrument makes sound when one part of it vibrates, moving to and fro very fast.
explanations.description: Every sound starts with something moving very fast and very small. Pluck a rubber band, and the band vibrates. Tap a box, and its sides vibrate in and out. Blow across a bottle, and the air inside it vibrates.
examples: A rubber band stretched over a tissue box: the band vibrates.
A box drum: the side of the box you tap vibrates.
A bottle hooter: the air inside the bottle vibrates.
Your voice: two small folds inside your throat vibrate. Put your fingers on your throat and hum to feel them.
explanations.art: Three small pictures: a blurry rubber band, a box side bulging in and out, and wavy lines of air inside a bottle.

explanations.context: This card is about why some sounds are high and some are low.
explanations.definition: Pitch is how high or low a sound is. Fast vibrations make high sounds. Slow vibrations make low sounds.
explanations.description: A high sound, like a squeak, comes from something vibrating very fast. A low sound, like a boom, comes from something vibrating more slowly. Hum a low note with your hand on your chest, and you feel a strong buzz. Hum a high note, and the buzz is weaker.
examples: A mouse squeaks high. A cow moos low.
A pressure cooker whistle is high. Thunder is low.
A small bell in a temple rings high. The big temple bell rings low.
explanations.art: A pitch ladder: a mouse and a whistle at the top, a person talking in the middle, a cow and thunder at the bottom.

explanations.concept: Why a big box sounds lower
explanations.context: This card is about the Big Box, Small Box test, where you tapped boxes of different sizes.
explanations.definition: When things are made of the same material and tapped the same way, the bigger one usually makes a lower sound.
explanations.description: When you tap a box, its side bends in and springs back, again and again. A small side is short and stiff, so it springs back very fast and makes a high 'tik'. A big side is wide and bends easily, so it moves more slowly and makes a low 'dhum'. A big box also holds more air, and that lowers the sound too.
examples: A big delivery carton booms. A matchbox ticks.
A tabla has two drums. The big one, called the bayan, gives the low sounds. The small one, the dayan, gives the high ones.
In a set of steel bowls, the biggest bowl rings lowest and the smallest rings highest.
explanations.art: A big carton with a wide side bending slowly in and out, next to a small box with a short side bending quickly.

explanations.concept: Low is not the same as loud
explanations.context: This card is about a mix-up many people make between low sounds and loud sounds.
explanations.definition: Loud or soft depends on how big the vibrations are. High or low depends on how fast they are.
explanations.description: Many people think a low sound is a loud sound, because big drums are often loud. But a gentle tap on the big carton is soft and still low. A hard tap on a matchbox is louder, but still high. How hard you hit changes how big the vibrations are, and the size of the box changes how fast they are.
examples: Tap the big carton with one finger, very gently. You hear a soft, low sound.
A whistle can be loud and high at the same time.
A cat purring is soft and low.
explanations.art: Two pictures of the same big carton: one with a gentle finger tap and small slow lines, one with a hard slap and big slow lines.

explanations.context: This card is about the Bottle Hooter, where you blow across the top of a bottle.
explanations.definition: When you blow across the mouth of a bottle, the air inside the bottle vibrates. Less air makes a higher note.
explanations.description: A bottle that looks empty is full of air. When your breath crosses the top, the air inside vibrates very fast, and that is the hoot. Pour in some water, and there is less air left to vibrate, so the hoot goes higher. A big empty bottle has lots of air, so it hoots low.
examples: An empty bottle gives a low hoot.
The same bottle, half full of water, gives a higher hoot.
A bamboo flute works the same way: the air inside the tube vibrates.
explanations.art: Three bottles: empty, a quarter full and half full of water, with wavy lines of air above the water getting shorter.

explanations.context: This card is about the difference between a beat and a rhythm, from the Name Rhythms activity.
explanations.definition: A beat is a steady pulse that repeats with the same gap each time. A rhythm is a pattern of sounds and gaps that fits over the beat.
explanations.description: The beat is like the ticking of a clock. It never speeds up or slows down in the middle. The rhythm is what you play on top of it. When you clap 'Mee-nak-shi' and then 'Kavya', the claps change, but the beat underneath stays the same.
examples: Your feet marching make a beat. Clapping your name while you march makes a rhythm.
A clock ticks a beat.
In a song, the words make rhythms over the beat.
explanations.art: A row of evenly spaced dots for the beat, and above it a pattern of claps, some close together and some with gaps.

explanations.concept: Tempo: how fast the beat goes
explanations.context: This card is about the Sleepy Song, Dancing Song test, where you counted pats in 15 seconds.
explanations.definition: Tempo is how fast the beat goes: how many beats there are in a fixed time.
explanations.description: You counted the beats of two songs for 15 seconds each. The lullaby usually gives far fewer pats than the dance song. Scientists who compared songs from many countries found that lullabies everywhere tend to be slow and soft.
examples: A lullaby: slow tempo.
A fast film dance song: fast tempo.
Rowers in a Kerala snake boat race pull their oars in time with the boat song.
explanations.art: A grandmother rocking a baby to a slow beat, next to a group of children dancing to a fast one.

explanations.concept: Tala: counting beats in a cycle
explanations.context: This card is about the Ta Ka Di Mi activity, where you counted Adi talam with your hands.
explanations.definition: In Indian classical music, a tala is a cycle of beats that repeats again and again.
explanations.description: Carnatic musicians, in South India, keep the tala with their hands. For Adi talam they clap, count three fingers, then clap and wave, then clap and wave. That makes 8 beats, and then they start again. Hindustani musicians, in North India, use talas too, and Teentaal has 16 beats.
examples: Adi talam: 8 beats in each cycle.
Teentaal: 16 beats in each cycle.
'Ta ka di mi' fits four syllables into four beats. 'Ta ki ta' makes a group of three.
explanations.art: A hand drawn eight times in a circle: clap, little finger, ring finger, middle finger, clap, wave, clap, wave, with the numbers 1 to 8.

explanations.concept: Do other animals feel a beat?
explanations.context: This card is about whether only humans move in time to music.
explanations.description: Humans and many other animals make sounds in rhythms, and frogs call in turns. Moving in time to music is rarer. In 2009, scientists filmed a cockatoo called Snowball bobbing his head and lifting his feet in time with a song. When the song was played faster or slower, Snowball often changed his speed to match. Scientists still argue about which animals can do this, and why.
examples: Snowball, a cockatoo, dancing to a pop song.
Ronan, a sea lion, bobbing her head to the beat.
Frogs at night calling in turns, so each one can be heard.

perspectives.explanation: They studied Snowball. They think animals that learn new sounds by copying, like parrots and humans, are the ones who can feel a beat and move to it.
They trained Ronan, a sea lion. Sea lions are not known to copy sounds, yet she learned to bob her head to the beat. So they think many more animals may be able to feel a beat.
They point out that a learned trick is not the same as enjoying music. Whether animals feel music the way we do is still an open question.

explanations.art: A white cockatoo with a yellow crest bobbing his head on a perch beside a speaker, and a sea lion bobbing her head by a pool.

agreed.text: Every sound starts with something vibrating: a string, a drum skin, the side of a box, or air.
agreed.evidence: You can see a plucked rubber band go blurry, and feel a box or your own throat buzz when it makes a sound.

agreed.text: Faster vibrations make higher sounds, and slower vibrations make lower sounds.
agreed.evidence: Scientists measure how many times a second things vibrate. High notes always have more vibrations each second than low notes.

agreed.text: Of two things with the same material and shape, the bigger one vibrates more slowly and makes the lower sound.
agreed.evidence: Big drums, big bells, big bowls and long strings all sound lower than small ones of the same kind. You tested this with boxes and steel bowls.

agreed.text: Most of the music people make, all over the world, has a steady beat.
agreed.evidence: Scientists who compared hundreds of songs from many countries found a steady beat in most of them.

challenging.claim: A low sound is a loud sound, and a high sound is a soft sound.
challenging.who: A very common idea, among children and grown-ups
challenging.for: Big drums are often both loud and low, and small bells are often soft and high.
challenging.against: Tap a big carton very gently. It is soft, but still low. A whistle is loud, but high. Loudness comes from how big the vibrations are. Pitch comes from how fast they are.
challenging.context: This card is about a common mix-up between low sounds and loud sounds.

challenging.claim: Only humans can move in time to a beat.
challenging.who: Many people believed this until about 2009
challenging.for: Most animals do not dance to music, even when they hear it every day.
challenging.against: Snowball the cockatoo and Ronan the sea lion both moved in time to the beat, and changed speed when the music changed. Scientists still argue about how many other animals can do it.
challenging.context: Can other animals keep a beat? This card looks at an old idea that turned out to be wrong.

challenging.claim: Playing music to plants makes them grow better.
challenging.who: Many gardeners, and some small studies
challenging.for: Plants do sense vibrations. Thale cress plants that were played the vibrations of caterpillars chewing made more of their bitter defence chemicals later, when caterpillars really ate them.
challenging.against: Careful tests of music and plant growth have given mixed results. Plants clearly sense and respond to vibrations, but there is no clear proof that songs help them grow.
challenging.context: This card is about whether plants respond to music. They do sense vibrations, but the music claim is not settled.

challenging.claim: Pythagoras found the musical notes by weighing a blacksmith's hammers.
challenging.who: An old story told by Nicomachus, a Greek writer, about 1,900 years ago
challenging.for: The story was copied in books for more than 1,000 years, and it does have some truth: bigger things often sound lower.
challenging.against: Around 1589, Vincenzo Galilei tested the numbers in the story with weights on strings, and they did not work. A hammer's sound depends on its size and shape, not on its weight alone.
challenging.context: This card is about a famous old story about music and numbers that turned out to be wrong when someone tested it.

big_questions.q: Why does a big box make a lower sound than a small box made of the same card?
big_questions.hint: Think about how fast each side can move in and out when you tap it.

big_questions.q: When you blew across the bottle, nothing seemed to move. So what was vibrating?
big_questions.hint: Was the bottle really empty? What was inside it?

big_questions.q: A clock goes tick, tick, tick, every tick the same. Why do so many people hear 'tick-tock'?
big_questions.hint: Our minds like to put beats into groups of two or three, even when every beat is the same.

big_questions.q: Is a sound high or low out in the air, or only in your ears and mind?
big_questions.hint: The box vibrates fast or slowly. Who decides that fast means 'high'?

big_questions.q: Why do people everywhere make music with a beat, and want to move when they hear one?
big_questions.hint: Think of rowers in a boat race, people marching, and a baby being rocked to sleep.

story.title: Kavya's Carton Drum
story.note: A made-up story. It is true that the ghatam is a clay-pot drum played in Carnatic concerts, that many ghatams are made in Manamadurai in Tamil Nadu, that Adi talam has 8 beats counted with a clap, three finger counts, and two claps with waves, and that Sukanya Ramgopal of Bengaluru is a famous ghatam player who began when very few women played it.
text: Kavya lived on the fourth floor of a tall building in Chennai, with Amma, Appa, her little brother Arjun and their Paati. Kavya was seven. Arjun was four. Paati was their grandmother. She had sung Carnatic songs all her life.

It was the morning of Pongal. The kitchen smelled of jaggery, ghee and cardamom, because Paati was making sweet pongal. Her two sisters were coming for lunch. Paati wanted the whole family to sing her favourite Pongal song together.
"But we have no mridangam," said Appa. "A song needs a drum."

Paati wiped her hands and looked at the pile of empty boxes by the door. There was the huge carton that the new fan had come in. There was a shoebox, a tissue box, and a little toothpaste box. "There are drums all around us," she said.
"Those are just boxes," said Arjun.

"A ghatam is just a clay pot," said Paati. "Musicians play it in big concerts, with their fingers and palms. Many of the best ghatams are made in a town called Manamadurai, near Madurai. One of the most famous ghatam players is a woman from Bengaluru called Sukanya Ramgopal. When she began, hardly any women played the ghatam. Now she has played in many countries."
Arjun grabbed the toothpaste box and tapped it with one finger. Tik, tik, tik.
Kavya giggled. "That's a mouse drum." She knelt by the big carton and slapped its side with her flat palm. DHUM. The deep sound filled the whole room. Arjun's eyes went wide.
Kavya tapped the shoebox. Tok. She tapped the toothpaste box again. Tik. Then the carton. Dhum. She frowned.
"They are all made of card," she said slowly. "But the big one sounds deep, and the little one sounds high. The shoebox is in the middle."

"Good listening," said Paati. "When you tap a box, its side moves in and out very fast. We say it vibrates. A big side is floppy, so it vibrates more slowly. Slow vibrations make a low sound. A small side is stiff, so it vibrates fast and makes a high sound."

Kavya made a band. The big carton was her drum. Arjun filled a plastic bottle with a handful of rice and screwed the cap on tight. That was his shaker. Paati stretched a long rubber band round the tissue box, over the hole, and gave it to Appa. "Pluck it," she said. Amma found an empty glass bottle and blew across the top. It gave a low hoot, like an owl.
"Ready?" said Kavya. "Go!"

Everyone played at once. Kavya banged fast. Arjun shook slowly, then very fast, then stopped to look at the rice. Appa plucked whenever he remembered. Amma hooted and then laughed so much she could not hoot at all. It sounded like a lorry full of pots going over a bump.

Paati held up her hand, and everyone stopped. "You each have a lovely sound," she said. "But you are all going at your own speed. Music needs a beat first. A beat is a steady pulse, like a clock ticking. Everybody listens to the same beat."

She began to clap and count, slowly and evenly. Clap. Little finger. Ring finger. Middle finger. Clap, and turn the hand over to wave. Clap, and wave. "That is Adi talam," she said. "Eight beats. Then we start again, round and round."

Kavya copied her. After two rounds she had it. Appa kept getting lost at the waves. "Appa, clap, and then just turn your hand over," said Kavya, and showed him with her own hand. "Clap, wave. Clap, wave." On the fourth round, Appa got it, and he looked very pleased with himself.

"Now say it like a drummer," said Paati. "Ta ka di mi, ta ka di mi." Kavya said it with her and hit the carton on every 'ta'. Dhum, ka, di, mi. Dhum, ka, di, mi. Arjun shook his bottle once on every beat. Appa plucked his rubber band on the claps. Amma hooted at the end of every round.
This time, the sounds did not crash into each other. They fitted together, like the pieces of a kolam.

When the doorbell rang, the band was ready. The great-aunts sat down, Paati began the Pongal song, and the family band played under it. The carton boomed, the bottle hissed, the rubber band twanged and the bottle hooted. One great-aunt clapped the tala along with them and nodded at Kavya.
Afterwards, Kavya sat with the carton on her lap and tapped it softly. Dhum. Still low, even when it was quiet.
"Paati," she said, "the big box always sings low and the little box always sings high. But it was the beat that made us a band."
story.epiphany: Big boxes sound low and small boxes sound high, because big sides vibrate more slowly. But different sounds only become music together when everyone follows one steady beat.

games.title: Echo Beat Cards
games.context: This is a game of copying rhythms. One player plays a rhythm from a secret card. Everyone else copies it, then guesses which card it was.

printables.title: 12 rhythm cards to cut out, with the sounds counted on the back

items.b: 2 knee pats, 1 clap and 1 silent beat

items.f: Say 'ta ka di mi'. Clap on 'ta', pat on the rest.
Say 'ta ki ta, ta ki ta'. Clap on the first 'ta' of each group, pat the rest.

rules: Cut out the 12 cards. Mix them and put them face down in a pile.
One player is the leader. A grown-up or the leader pats a slow, steady beat on their knees to start.
The leader takes the top card secretly and plays its rhythm twice, in time with the beat.
Everyone else copies the rhythm. Each player who copies it right gets 1 point.
The leader puts the card face up with two other cards from the pile. Players point to the card they think was played. Each right guess gets 1 point.
The next player becomes the leader. When everyone has led three times, the player with the most points wins.

setup.art: Twelve small paper cards fanned out on a mat, each with a rhythm written on it, such as 'clap, clap, rest, clap'.
setup.caption: 1. Cut out the cards and mix them face down.

setup.art: A girl holding a secret card and clapping, while her father and brother listen and get ready to copy.
setup.caption: 2. The leader plays a card. Everyone copies it.

flow.context: This is the first step of Echo Beat Cards. You cut out rhythm cards and set up the game.
flow.do: 1. Cut out the 12 cards. 2. Read one card aloud and play it together, so everyone knows what clap, pat, stamp and rest mean.
flow.say: A rest is a silent beat. You do nothing, but you still count it. Let's try one card together.
flow.kid: A rest means a silent beat. Count it, but make no sound.
flow.parent: Rests are the hardest part. Nod your head on a rest, so everyone feels the silent beat.

flow.do: 1. Take turns to lead. 2. Keep a steady beat going on your knees. 3. Write the points on the score sheet.
flow.say: Listen to the leader. Copy the rhythm exactly. Then, which card was it?
flow.kid: Listen. Copy the rhythm. Then point to the card.

ask.q: How did you know which card it was?
good: I heard where the rest was.

flow.parent: If a child loses the beat, stop and pat the beat together for a few seconds before trying again.

flow.do: Add up the points. Ask which card was the hardest to copy.
flow.say: Which card was hardest? Why?
flow.kid: Which card was hardest? Why?

check.q: Ananya plays 'clap, rest, clap, rest'. How many sounds does she make?
check.why: She claps twice. The two rests are silent beats. They are counted, but they make no sound.

games.title: Pattern Train: build a rhythm that repeats
games.context: This is a game of building rhythm patterns. Players lay sound cards in a line, like the carriages of a train, so that a pattern repeats. Then everyone plays the train in time with the beat.
rules: Cut out the 20 sound cards and spread them face up.
The first player builds a train of 8 cards in a line. The train must be a pattern that repeats, such as clap, pat, clap, pat, clap, pat, clap, pat.
Everyone checks that the pattern really repeats. If it does not, the builder fixes it.
A grown-up pats a steady beat. Everyone plays the train together, one card on each beat, from the first card to the last.
If everyone plays the whole train without stopping, the builder gets 1 point.
The next player changes the train into a new repeating pattern, by swapping as few cards as they can. Play it again.
After four trains each, the player with the most points wins.

setup.art: A line of 8 paper cards on the floor reading clap, clap, stamp, rest, clap, clap, stamp, rest, drawn like train carriages.
setup.caption: 1. Build a train of 8 cards that repeats.

setup.art: A family sitting in a row, clapping and stamping together while a grandmother pats the beat.
setup.caption: 2. Play the train together, one card on each beat.

flow.context: This is the first step of Pattern Train. You build a rhythm from sound cards that repeats, like a pattern.
flow.do: 1. Cut out the 20 cards. 2. Build the first train together: clap, pat, clap, pat, clap, pat, clap, pat.
flow.say: A pattern repeats in the same order. Clap, pat, clap, pat. What comes next?
flow.kid: Clap, pat, clap, pat. What comes next?
flow.parent: Patterns with two parts are easiest, like clap, pat. Patterns with three or four parts, like clap, clap, stamp, rest, are harder.

flow.do: 1. Take turns to build or change the train. 2. Pat a steady beat while everyone plays it.
flow.say: Is this train a pattern that repeats? Let's check, then play it on the beat.
flow.kid: Build your train. Does it repeat? Now play it on the beat.

ask.q: How do you know your train repeats?
good: The first half is the same as the second half.
Clap, clap, stamp comes again and again.

flow.parent: A train of 8 can hold a 2-part pattern four times, or a 4-part pattern twice. A 3-part pattern does not fit exactly into 8 cards. If your child spots this, praise it.

flow.do: Count the points. Ask which train was the most fun to play.
flow.say: Which train sounded best? Why?
flow.kid: Which train sounded best? Why?

check.q: Deepa builds: clap, stamp, clap, stamp, clap, stamp, clap. What should the 8th card be?
check.why: The pattern is clap, stamp, again and again. After a clap comes a stamp, so the 8th card is stamp.

experiments.title: Big Box, Small Box: which makes the deepest sound?
experiments.context: In this experiment you tap four empty boxes of very different sizes in exactly the same way, and listen for which sounds high and which sounds low. Then you check with steel bowls.
experiments.question: If boxes are all made of card and tapped the same way, does the size of a box change how high or low it sounds?
experiments.predict: Guess first. Which box will make the deepest sound: the smallest, the biggest, or will they all sound the same? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Every box is empty, with its lid taped shut, and lies on the floor on its biggest side. Every tap is the same: one finger, dropped onto the middle of the top. Only the size of the box changes. We tap each box twice, because one tap can sound different by mistake.

materials.item: 4 empty cardboard boxes of very different sizes: an empty matchbox (no matches in it) or small medicine box, a toothpaste or tea box, a shoebox, and a big delivery carton
cellotape, to keep each lid shut
3 steel bowls or dabbas from one stacking set: a big one, a middle one and a small one
a steel spoon
a folded towel or cloth, to stand the bowls on
paper and a pencil, for the results table

schedule.what: Guess, tap four boxes the same way, feel the big box buzz, play the eyes-shut round, check with steel bowls, and talk about why.

experiments.record: Fill in the results table. Draw the four boxes on a ladder: the deepest at the bottom, the highest at the top. Write how many boxes you named right in the eyes-shut round.

setup.art: Four empty boxes in a row on a floor mat, from a tiny matchbox to a big delivery carton, each with its lid taped shut.
setup.caption: 1. Line up four boxes, smallest to biggest. Tape the lids shut.

setup.art: A child's single finger dropping onto the middle of the top of a shoebox, with a small arrow showing the tap.
setup.caption: 2. Tap the middle of the top with one finger. Same tap every time.

setup.art: A child with eyes shut and back turned, while a grown-up taps one of the boxes behind her.
setup.caption: 3. Eyes shut: which box made that sound?

setup.art: Three steel bowls from one set, big, middle and small, standing on a folded towel, and a hand tapping the rim of one with a spoon.
setup.caption: 4. Check with steel bowls: tap each rim with a spoon.

flow.context: This is the first step of the Big Box, Small Box test. You guess which box will make the deepest sound before you tap any of them.
flow.do: 1. Put the four boxes in a row, from smallest to biggest. 2. Draw the results table with four rows. 3. Ask your child to guess for each box.
flow.say: We are going to tap each box in exactly the same way. Which one will make the deepest sound? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Look at the four boxes. Which will sound deepest? Why do you think so?

good: The big one, because big drums are deep.
The small one, because it is hard.
All the same, because they are all card.

flow.parent: Any guess is fine if it has a reason. Write each guess in the table. Do not explain anything yet.

flow.do: 1. Tape each lid shut. 2. Lay each box on the floor on its biggest side. 3. Show the tap: one finger, dropped onto the middle of the top.
flow.say: Every box must get the same tap, in the same place. Why do you think that matters?
flow.kid: Tape the lids shut. Lay each box flat. Tap the middle with one finger.

ask.q: Why must every tap be the same?
good: So only the box is different.

flow.parent: A tile or stone floor works well. On a soft mattress the boxes hardly sound at all.

flow.do: 1. Your child taps each box twice, from smallest to biggest. 2. After each box, they say a sound word for it: tik, tok, dum or dhum. 3. Write the word and 'high', 'middle' or 'low' in the table.
flow.say: Tap the smallest box. Listen. Is it high or low? Now the next one. Say a sound word for each.
flow.kid: Tap each box twice. Listen hard. Is it high or low?

ask.q: What did you hear as the boxes got bigger?
good: The little one went tik and the big one went dhum.

flow.parent: The matchbox gives a high, short 'tik'. The big carton gives a deep 'dhum', like a big drum. If two boxes sound almost the same, they are probably close in size. Use boxes that are very different.

flow.do: 1. Your child rests the fingertips of one hand lightly on the top of the big carton. 2. With the other hand, they slap the side of the carton once with a flat palm. 3. Do the same with the smallest box.
flow.say: Put your fingers lightly on top of the big carton. Now slap its side. What do your fingers feel?
flow.kid: Fingers on top of the big box. Slap its side. What do you feel?
flow.parent: The carton's top buzzes under the fingers. That buzz is the card vibrating. The small box buzzes too, but too fast and too little to feel well.

flow.do: 1. Your child shuts their eyes and turns their back. 2. Tap one box, chosen at random, twice. 3. Your child names the box. 4. Do this 4 times, and count the right answers.
flow.say: Eyes shut. I will tap one box. Can you tell which one, just from the sound?
flow.kid: Shut your eyes. Listen. Which box was it?
flow.parent: Most children of 7 get 3 or 4 right, because big and small boxes sound so different. The two middle boxes are the easiest to mix up.

flow.do: 1. Stand the three steel bowls on a folded towel. 2. Your child taps the rim of each gently with the spoon. 3. Ask which rings lowest and which highest.
flow.say: These bowls are all the same steel, from one set. Only the size is different. Which rings lowest?
flow.kid: Tap each bowl with the spoon. Which rings lowest? Which rings highest?
flow.parent: The biggest bowl rings lowest and the smallest rings highest. This shows the size rule works for steel too, not only card. Tap gently, so the spoon does not dent or chip anything.

flow.do: 1. Ask your child what they found, and how they know. 2. Only then, explain why bigger boxes sound lower.
flow.say: What did you find out? What did you hear that tells you so? Why do you think the big box sounded deeper?
flow.kid: What did you find? Which sounded deepest? Why, do you think?

ask.q: What did you find, and how do you know?
good: The bigger the box, the deeper the sound. The carton went dhum and the matchbox went tik.
The biggest bowl rang lowest too.

flow.parent: After your child has said what they think, explain: when you tap a box, its side bends in and springs back again and again. That is vibrating. A big side is floppy, so it vibrates more slowly. Slow vibrations make a low sound.

check.q: Meena taps a box and hears a high 'tik'. She wants a lower sound. Which box should she tap next, in the same way?
check.why: A bigger box has bigger sides that vibrate more slowly, so the sound is lower. Tapping harder only makes the same sound louder.

experiments.title: Sleepy Song, Dancing Song: how fast is the beat?
experiments.context: In this experiment you pat your knees along with two songs, a lullaby and a dance song, and count the pats in 15 seconds. You find out how different their tempos are.
experiments.question: Does a lullaby have a slower beat than a dance song? How many beats does each have in 15 seconds?
experiments.predict: Guess first. Which song will give you more pats in 15 seconds, the lullaby or the dance song? About how many for each? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: We count for the same time, 15 seconds, for both songs. The same person pats, one pat on each beat. We count each song twice, because one count can go wrong.

materials.item: a phone, to play the two songs
a clock with a seconds hand, or a second phone with a timer
a slow lullaby your family knows, such as 'Omanathinkal kidavo' in Malayalam, 'Aararo aariraro' in Tamil, or 'Chanda mama door ke' in Hindi
a fast dance song your family likes
paper and a pencil for tally marks

schedule.what: Guess, find the beat of each song, count the pats in 15 seconds twice for each song, and compare.

experiments.record: Fill in the results table. Draw one bar for each song, as tall as its number of pats.

setup.art: A child sitting cross-legged, patting both knees, while a phone on the floor plays a song.
setup.caption: 1. Play the song. Pat your knees on every beat.

setup.art: A grown-up watching the seconds hand of a wall clock and making tally marks on paper, while the child pats.
setup.caption: 2. A grown-up times 15 seconds and makes a mark for every pat.

setup.art: A sheet of paper with two rows of tally marks, a short row for the lullaby and a long row for the dance song.
setup.caption: 3. Count the marks for each song.

flow.context: This is the first step of the Sleepy Song, Dancing Song test. You guess how many beats each song has in 15 seconds.
flow.do: 1. Choose the lullaby and the dance song. 2. Draw the results table. 3. Ask your child to guess the number of pats for each.
flow.say: We will pat along to a lullaby and a dance song for 15 seconds each. Which will give more pats? How many? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Which song has a faster beat? Guess how many pats for each. Why?

good: The dance song, because dancing is fast.
The same, because a beat is a beat.

flow.parent: Fifteen seconds is about as long as it takes to count slowly to fifteen. Write both guesses in the table.

flow.do: 1. Play the lullaby. 2. Pat both knees together on every beat, with your child. 3. Then play the dance song and do the same.
flow.say: Let's find the beat. It is the steady pulse you could rock a baby to, or march to. Pat it with me.
flow.kid: Listen for the steady beat. Pat your knees on every beat.
flow.parent: Some children pat on every word instead of every beat. Pat with them until they settle into a steady pulse.

flow.do: 1. Play the lullaby. 2. When the seconds hand reaches 12, say 'Go'. 3. Make one tally mark for each pat. 4. Say 'Stop' after 15 seconds. 5. Do the same for the dance song.
flow.say: Pat on every beat. I will make a mark each time you pat. Ready? Go!
flow.kid: Pat on every beat until the grown-up says stop.
flow.parent: A lullaby usually gives about 15 to 20 pats in 15 seconds. A fast dance song often gives 25 to 35. Your numbers will depend on your songs.

flow.do: 1. Count each song a second time, the same way. 2. Add the tallies up and write the numbers in the table.
flow.say: Let's count each song once more. Do we get nearly the same number again?
flow.kid: Count each song again. Is it nearly the same?
flow.parent: The two counts for one song should be close. If one is about half the other, your child patted on every other beat that time. That is fine: count again.

flow.do: 1. Ask what your child found, and how they know. 2. Then tell them the word for how fast a beat goes: tempo.
flow.say: Which song had more pats in 15 seconds? How many more? Why do you think a lullaby is slow?
flow.kid: Which song had more pats? Why is a lullaby slow?

ask.q: Why might a lullaby be slow?

flow.parent: How fast a beat goes is called its tempo. Scientists who compared songs from many countries found that lullabies everywhere tend to be slow and soft.

check.q: Thenmozhi pats along to a slow lullaby for 15 seconds. About how many pats will she make?
check.why: A slow lullaby gives about 15 to 20 pats in 15 seconds. 6 is too few for a steady beat, and 40 is too many, even for a fast dance song.

activities.title: Name Rhythms: find the beat, then clap your name
activities.context: In this activity you march to a steady beat, then clap the rhythm of your name on top of it. You find out the difference between a beat and a rhythm.

materials.item: nothing but your hands and feet, and some space to march

schedule.what: March to a steady beat, clap family names, then clap names while the beat goes on.

activities.record: Write three family names and draw a dot for each clap under each name.

setup.art: A girl and her grandmother marching round a small living room, stepping in time.
setup.caption: 1. March round the room to a steady beat.

setup.art: A girl clapping, with the name 'Mee-nak-shi' split into three parts and a dot under each part.
setup.caption: 2. Clap your name: one clap for each part.

flow.context: This is the first step of Name Rhythms. You march to a steady beat, like a clock ticking.
flow.do: 1. Say 'tick, tick, tick, tick' slowly and evenly, like a clock. 2. March round the room together, one step on each tick.
flow.say: Let's march like a clock. One step on every tick. Tick, tick, tick, tick.
flow.kid: March round the room. One step on every tick.

ask.q: Did the ticks get faster or slower, or stay the same?

flow.parent: Keep your ticks very even, about one each second. This steady pulse is called the beat.

flow.do: 1. Say your child's name in parts, clapping on each part. 2. Do the same with three family names. For example, Ka-vya is 2 claps and Mee-nak-shi is 3.
flow.say: Now clap your name. One clap for each part. Ka-vya: clap, clap. How many claps is your name?
flow.kid: Clap your name. One clap for each part. How many claps?
flow.parent: Clapping the parts of words is called clapping the rhythm. Different names make different rhythms.

flow.do: 1. March and say 'tick, tick' again. 2. While the beat goes on, your child claps and says one name after another.
flow.say: Keep marching on the beat. Now clap names on top of it. Does your marching change?
flow.kid: Keep marching. Clap names at the same time. Do your feet change?
flow.parent: The marching stays the same, and the claps change. The steady marching is the beat. The pattern of claps is the rhythm.

check.q: Lakshmi marches and claps her name at the same time. Which one is the beat?
check.why: The beat is the steady pulse that never changes, like her steps. The claps of her name are a rhythm that fits over the beat.

activities.title: Ta Ka Di Mi: speak like a drum, and count Adi talam
activities.context: In this activity you say drum syllables out loud, the way South Indian drummers do, and count Adi talam, a cycle of 8 beats, with your hands.

materials.item: your hands and your voice

schedule.what: Say ta ka di mi and ta ki ta on a beat, then count Adi talam with claps, fingers and waves.

activities.record: Draw the 8 hand shapes of Adi talam in a circle, numbered 1 to 8.

setup.art: A girl patting her knees and saying 'ta ka di mi', with the four syllables written above her in a row.
setup.caption: 1. Pat the beat. Say ta ka di mi.

setup.art: Eight small drawings of a hand in a circle: clap, little finger, ring finger, middle finger, clap, wave, clap, wave, numbered 1 to 8.
setup.caption: 2. Count Adi talam: 8 beats with claps, fingers and waves.

flow.context: This is the first step of Ta Ka Di Mi. You say drum syllables in time with a steady beat.
flow.do: 1. Pat your knees slowly and evenly together. 2. Say one syllable on each pat: ta, ka, di, mi. 3. Repeat it again and again. 4. Then clap only on 'ta'.
flow.say: Drummers in South India say their rhythms out loud. Say it with me on every pat: ta, ka, di, mi.
flow.kid: Pat your knees. Say ta, ka, di, mi. One sound on each pat.
flow.parent: Speaking drum syllables like this is called konnakol. 'Ta ka di mi' is a group of four.

flow.do: 1. Keep patting. 2. Now say 'ta ki ta' over and over, one syllable on each pat. 3. Clap on every 'ta'.
flow.say: Now try a group of three: ta, ki, ta. Clap on the first 'ta' each time. Does the clap come at a new place?
flow.kid: Now say ta, ki, ta. Clap on the first ta.
flow.parent: In groups of four the clap comes every fourth pat. In groups of three it comes every third pat. The pats stay the same, but the pattern changes.

flow.do: 1. Show your child Adi talam, slowly. 2. Clap. Touch your little finger to your thumb, then the ring finger, then the middle finger. 3. Clap, then turn your hand over to wave. 4. Clap, and wave again. 5. Do it together four times.
flow.say: This is Adi talam. Clap, one, two, three. Clap, wave. Clap, wave. That is 8 beats. Then start again.
flow.kid: Clap. Little finger, ring finger, middle finger. Clap, wave. Clap, wave.

ask.q: How many beats are in one round?

flow.parent: The finger counts are done on the palm-up hand, touching each finger to the thumb, or tapping them on the other palm. Many children mix up the waves at first. Slow down and say the beat numbers aloud.

flow.do: 1. You keep counting Adi talam. 2. Your child says 'ta ka di mi, ta ka di mi', one syllable on each beat.
flow.say: I will count the tala. You say ta ka di mi twice in each round. Do they fit?
flow.kid: Say ta ka di mi twice. Does it fit one round?
flow.parent: Eight syllables fit exactly into the 8 beats of Adi talam.

check.q: Thenmozhi says 'ta ka di mi' two times while her Paati counts one round of Adi talam. How many syllables does she say?
check.why: 'Ta ka di mi' has 4 syllables. Two times 4 is 8, and Adi talam has 8 beats, so they fit exactly.

activities.title: Tissue-box Ektara: a one-string instrument
activities.context: In this activity you make a one-string instrument from a tissue box and a rubber band, and play a steady beat on it while you sing, like the Baul singers of Bengal.

materials.item: an empty tissue box with a hole in the top, or a shoebox with a hole about the size of a fist cut in the lid by a grown-up
a long rubber band, or two shorter ones looped together, long enough to go round the box the long way
a pencil

schedule.what: Build the ektara, find out what vibrates, and play a steady beat on it while singing.

activities.record: Draw your ektara and draw wavy lines on the part that vibrates.

setup.art: A rubber band stretched the long way round a tissue box, right over the hole, with a pencil slipped under the band near one end.
setup.caption: 1. Stretch the band round the box, over the hole. Slip a pencil under it.

setup.art: A child plucking the band over the hole with one finger, the band blurry, while singing.
setup.caption: 2. Pluck it over the hole, on the beat, while you sing.

flow.context: This is the first step of the Tissue-box Ektara. You build a one-string instrument from a box and a rubber band.
flow.do: 1. Stretch the rubber band round the box the long way, so it passes over the hole. 2. Slip the pencil under the band near one end of the box, so the band lifts up off the box.
flow.say: An ektara is a real instrument with just one string. 'Ek' means one, and 'tar' means string. Let's make one.
flow.kid: Stretch the band round the box, over the hole. Put the pencil under it.
flow.parent: The Baul singers of Bengal sing and dance while they pluck an ektara in a steady beat. A real ektara has a gourd for a body and a bamboo neck.

flow.do: 1. Pluck the band over the hole with one finger. 2. Look closely at the band. 3. Rest a fingertip lightly on the box while you pluck.
flow.say: Pluck it. Look at the band. What does it look like? Now feel the box while you pluck.
flow.kid: Pluck the band. Look at it. Then feel the box.

ask.q: What did the band look like when you plucked it?

flow.parent: The band goes blurry because it is vibrating. The box buzzes a little too, because it vibrates along with the band.

flow.do: 1. Sing a song your child knows. 2. Your child plucks the band once on every beat. 3. Then try plucking twice on every beat.
flow.say: Let's sing. You pluck on every beat, like a Baul singer. Keep it steady, even if the words change.
flow.kid: Sing a song. Pluck once on every beat. Keep it steady.
flow.parent: Keeping the plucks steady while singing is hard at first. Pat the beat on your knee to help.

activities.title: Bottle Hooter: make a bottle sing
activities.context: In this activity you blow across the top of a bottle to make it hoot. Then you add water and listen to the hoot change.

materials.item: an empty glass bottle or a plastic water bottle, 500 millilitres to 1 litre, with a narrow neck
a jug of water

activities.safety: If you use a glass bottle, keep it on a towel on the floor, so it cannot fall and break. Wash the bottle's mouth before another person blows on it.

schedule.what: Learn to hoot an empty bottle, then add water a little at a time and listen.

activities.record: Draw the bottle with no water, a little water, and half full. Next to each, write 'low', 'middle' or 'high'.

setup.art: A child with their lower lip touching the edge of a bottle's mouth, blowing gently straight across the top.
setup.caption: 1. Lower lip on the edge. Blow gently across the top.

setup.art: Three bottles in a row: empty, a quarter full and half full of water.
setup.caption: 2. Add water. Listen to the hoot change.

flow.context: This is the first step of the Bottle Hooter. You learn to make an empty bottle hoot.
flow.do: 1. A grown-up tries first. 2. Rest your lower lip on the edge of the bottle's mouth. 3. Blow gently, straight across the top, not into the bottle.
flow.say: Rest your lip on the edge and blow gently across the top, as if you are saying 'poo' very softly.
flow.kid: Lip on the edge. Blow softly across the top. Keep trying!
flow.parent: It takes most people several tries. Tilt the bottle a little away from your mouth, and blow more gently, not harder. If your child cannot do it, you hoot and they listen.

flow.do: 1. Pour water into the bottle until it is about a quarter full. 2. Hoot again. 3. Fill it to half and hoot again.
flow.say: Now we put some water in. Will the hoot be higher, lower or the same? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Guess first. Then hoot again with water inside. Higher or lower?
flow.parent: The hoot goes higher as you add water. The hoot is the air inside the bottle vibrating. Water leaves less air to vibrate, and less air vibrates faster.

flow.do: Ask your child what is vibrating to make the hoot.
flow.say: Nothing in the bottle seems to move. So what is vibrating to make the hoot?
flow.kid: Nothing seems to move. So what is vibrating?

check.q: Anjali, a girl in Kochi, blows across an empty bottle and it hoots. What is vibrating?
check.why: The bottle looks empty, but it is full of air. Her breath makes that air vibrate very fast, and that is the hoot.

projects.title: Our Box Band Concert
projects.context: In this project your family makes a band from boxes, bottles and rubber bands, practises one song on a steady beat, and plays a short concert.

materials.item: a big cardboard carton, for the low drum
a small box, for the high drum
a tissue box and a long rubber band, for the ektara
a small plastic bottle with a cap, and a handful of rice or dal, for a shaker
an empty bottle, for a hooter
cellotape, and paper and crayons to decorate

schedule.what: Build and decorate the instruments. Choose a song and who plays what.
Practise the song on a steady beat with Adi talam, then play the concert for the family.

projects.record: Draw your band and write the name of each instrument, who played it, and whether it sounded high, middle or low.

setup.art: A floor covered in home-made instruments: a decorated carton drum, a small box drum, a tissue-box ektara, a rice shaker bottle and a glass bottle.
setup.caption: 1. Build and decorate the instruments.

setup.art: A family sitting in a half circle playing the instruments while a grandmother claps the tala, and two neighbours watching.
setup.caption: 2. Practise on one beat, then play the concert.

flow.context: This is day 1 of Our Box Band Concert. You build the instruments and plan the song.
flow.do: 1. Tape the boxes shut and decorate them. 2. Make the ektara. 3. Put a handful of rice in the small bottle and screw the cap on tight. 4. Choose a song and who plays what.
flow.say: Every band needs a low sound, a high sound and a beat. Which instrument will you play? Which song shall we play?
flow.kid: Build the instruments. Decorate them. Choose your instrument and a song.
flow.parent: Check the shaker cap is tight, so rice does not spill. A song the whole family knows works best.

flow.do: 1. Count Adi talam together for one round. 2. Play the song, with everyone keeping to the beat. 3. Practise twice. 4. Play the concert.
flow.say: First the beat. Clap, one, two, three, clap, wave, clap, wave. Now everyone plays on the beat.
flow.kid: Listen for the beat first. Then play on the beat.

ask.q: What helped the band stay together?

flow.parent: Give the low drum the main beat. The others can play on some beats, or between them. Keep the tempo slow for the first practice.

challenges.title: A Band of Three: high, middle and low
challenges.context: This is a design challenge. You make three instruments from things at home: one that sounds high, one middle and one low. Then you play them together on one beat.
challenges.problem: Can you make three instruments from boxes, bottles and rubber bands, so that one sounds high, one sounds in the middle and one sounds low?
constraints: Use only things already at home: boxes, bottles, rubber bands, tape, water, steel bowls and spoons.
Everyone listening must agree which instrument is high, middle and low.
You must be able to play all three on the same steady beat.
materials: empty cardboard boxes of different sizes
plastic or glass bottles and water
steel bowls and a steel spoon
general: Use three boxes of very different sizes: the biggest is the low drum and the smallest is the high one.
Use three bottles with different amounts of water: the emptiest hoots lowest.
Use three steel bowls from one set, tapped with a spoon: the biggest rings lowest.
creative: Mix the kinds: a big carton for the low sound, a hooting bottle for the middle, and a small steel bowl for the high one.
Stretch rubber bands over boxes of different sizes and compare their twangs.
Tie three steel spoons of different sizes on strings from a coat hanger, and tap them like bells.
challenges.your_turn: Make your own band of three. Ask someone to listen with their eyes shut and say which is high, middle and low. If two sound alike, change one: use a bigger box, or add or pour out water.

setup.art: A big carton, a half-full bottle and a small steel bowl lined up on a mat, with the words low, middle and high under them.
setup.caption: 1. Choose a low, a middle and a high instrument.

setup.art: A boy with his eyes shut, pointing up for a high sound, while his sister plays the small steel bowl.
setup.caption: 2. A listener, eyes shut, says which is high, middle or low.

flow.context: This is the first step of A Band of Three. You read the challenge and plan your three instruments.
flow.do: Read the challenge together. Lay out the boxes, bottles, bands and bowls you have.
flow.say: We need one high, one middle and one low instrument. Which things do you think will sound lowest? Why?
flow.kid: Which things will sound lowest? Which highest? Why?

flow.do: Let your child build and test. Help with tape and with pouring water.
flow.say: Try each one. Is it high, middle or low? Change one if two sound the same.
flow.kid: Try each one. High, middle or low? Change one if two match.
flow.parent: Let your child try their own ideas first. If they are stuck, remind them of the Big Box test and the Bottle Hooter.

flow.do: 1. A listener shuts their eyes. 2. Your child plays each instrument. 3. The listener says high, middle or low. 4. Then play all three together on one beat.
flow.say: Let's test your band. Then play all three together while I count Adi talam.
flow.kid: Play each one for the listener. Then play all three on the beat.

ask.q: Which change made the biggest difference to the sound?
good: Adding lots of water to the bottle.

quiz.p: Meenakshi stretches a rubber band over a tissue box and plucks it. What vibrates to make the sound?
quiz.why: The band moves to and fro very fast. Look closely and it goes blurry. The box vibrates along with it, which makes the sound louder.

quiz.p: Which of these makes a high sound?
quiz.why: A squeak is thin and sharp, so it is high. Thunder and a moo are deep, so they are low.

quiz.p: Farhan taps a matchbox and a big delivery carton in exactly the same way. Which one sounds lower?
quiz.why: The carton's big sides vibrate more slowly, and slow vibrations make a low sound. Choosing 'the same' means thinking only about the material, not the size.

quiz.p: Why does a big carton sound lower than a small box?
opts: Its big sides vibrate more slowly
The card in it is a different colour
quiz.why: A big side is wide and floppy, so it moves in and out more slowly. Slow vibrations make low sounds. Loudness is a different thing.

quiz.p: Lakshmi taps the big carton very, very gently with one finger. What does she hear?
quiz.why: A gentle tap makes small vibrations, so the sound is soft. The carton's sides still vibrate slowly, so it is still low. Low does not mean loud.

quiz.p: Anjali hoots an empty bottle. Then she pours in water until the bottle is half full. What happens to the hoot?
quiz.why: The hoot is the air inside vibrating. Water leaves less air, and less air vibrates faster, so the hoot goes higher.

quiz.p: Which of these is a beat?
opts: A steady pulse with the same gap each time, like a clock ticking
The loudest sound in a song
quiz.why: A beat repeats steadily. Loudness and highness are about other things.

quiz.p: Kavya claps her name: Ka-vya, 2 claps. How many claps is 'Mee-nak-shi'?
quiz.why: Mee-nak-shi has three parts, so it is three claps. That pattern of claps is the name's rhythm.

quiz.p: How many beats are in one round of Adi talam?
quiz.why: Adi talam has 8 beats: a clap, three finger counts, a clap and a wave, and a clap and a wave. Teentaal, in Hindustani music, is the one with 16.

quiz.p: Bidisha pats along to a lullaby and then to a dance song, for 15 seconds each. Which one usually gives more pats?
opts: Every song gives the same number
quiz.why: A dance song usually has a faster tempo, so it has more beats in 15 seconds. Lullabies are slow, to help a baby calm down.

quiz.p: Snowball is a cockatoo in America. What did scientists see Snowball do?
opts: Bob his head in time with music, and change speed when the music changed
quiz.why: Snowball danced to the beat. When the song was played faster or slower, he often changed his speed to match.

quiz.p: Arjun wants to find out if the size of a box changes its sound. Which test is fair?
opts: Tap every box the same way, in the same place
Tap the small box gently and the big box hard
quiz.why: In a fair test only one thing changes, here the size of the box. If the taps are different, you cannot tell what made the sound change.

items.p: Kamala plucks a rubber band on a box. How can she tell that the band is vibrating?
items.why: A strong answer says the band moves to and fro so fast that it looks blurry.

items.p: True or false: every sound starts with something vibrating.
items.why: True. A plucked band goes blurry, and your throat buzzes when you hum.

items.p: Draw a line from each instrument to the part that vibrates.
pairs: two small folds in your throat
items.why: Every instrument has a part that vibrates. A strong answer can point to it on each one.

items.p: Remember the Big Box, Small Box test. Draw your four boxes on a ladder: the deepest sound at the bottom, the highest at the top. Write the sound word next to each.
items.a: The big carton at the bottom with 'dhum', then the shoebox, then the toothpaste box, and the matchbox at the top with 'tik'.
items.why: A strong drawing puts the boxes in order of size, biggest at the bottom, because bigger boxes sounded lower.
items.art: An empty ladder with four rungs for drawing.

items.p: Say it, and a grown-up writes it down: in the Big Box test, which box sounded deepest? What did you hear that shows it?
items.a: The big carton sounded deepest. It went 'dhum', and the matchbox went 'tik'.
items.why: A strong answer names the box and gives evidence from the test: the sound words or the order heard.

items.p: Sort these sounds into high and low.
items: the whistle of a pressure cooker
items.why: Squeaks, whistles and cheeps are thin and sharp, so they are high. Big bells, thunder and big drums are deep, so they are low.

items.p: Three steel bowls come from one set: big, middle and small. Put them in order from the lowest ring to the highest.
items.why: They are all the same steel, so only size changes the sound. The biggest bowl vibrates most slowly and rings lowest.

items.p: A beat is a ___ pulse that repeats, like a clock ticking.
items.why: A beat keeps the same gap every time. It does not speed up or slow down in the middle.

items.p: Clap the name 'Ar-jun', and then the name 'Ka-ma-la'. How many claps is that altogether?
items.why: Ar-jun is 2 claps and Ka-ma-la is 3 claps. 2 and 3 make 5.

items.p: Label the tissue-box ektara: rubber band, box, hole, pencil.
a: rubber band: the part you pluck, which vibrates
box: it vibrates along with the band and makes it louder
hole: where you pluck, over the open box
pencil: it lifts the band off the box
items.why: A strong answer names each part and says what the band does: it vibrates.
items.art: A tissue box with a rubber band stretched over its hole and a pencil under the band, with four empty label lines.

items.p: Three friends are making music for a baby's naming day. They want the baby to stay calm.

views.says: Play the big carton drum gently. Its sound is low and calm.
Hoot the bottle softly. A soft hoot is the gentlest sound.
Shake the rice bottle slowly, on a slow beat, like a lullaby.

items.ask: Who do you agree with? Give one reason from your own tests. Then say one thing another friend has right.
items.a: A strong answer picks a side and gives a reason. Kavya is right that a gentle tap on the carton is soft and low. Ananya is right that soft sounds are calmer. Farhan is right that a slow tempo, like a lullaby's, helps a baby calm down.
items.why: Being calm depends on being soft and on a slow tempo, more than on being high or low. Each friend has part of it.

items.p: Revathi, a girl in Madurai, rings the big bell at the temple and then her small hand bell at home. Which one rings lower?
opts: Both the same, because both are bells
items.why: Both are bells, but the bigger one vibrates more slowly, so it rings lower.

items.p: Many people think a big drum sounds low because it is loud. How could you test whether that is true?
items.a: Tap the big carton very gently, so it is soft. If it still sounds low, then low does not come from being loud.
items.why: A strong answer changes only how hard you tap, and listens for whether the sound is still low.

items.p: Draw the rhythm of your full name. Draw one big dot for each clap.
items.a: A row of dots, one for each part of the child's name. For example, 'Lak-shmi Raj' has 3 dots.
items.why: A strong drawing has one dot for each part of the name, in order.
items.art: An empty strip for drawing dots.

items.p: Which is the odd one out?
items.why: The ektara, veena and tambura all have a string that vibrates. In the bottle hooter, the air vibrates.

items.p: True or false: two people can clap different rhythms and still keep the same beat.
items.why: True. In Name Rhythms, your steps stayed the same while the claps changed. The steps were the beat and the claps were the rhythm.

items.p: How fast a beat goes is called its ___.
items.why: A lullaby has a slow tempo and a dance song has a fast tempo.

items.p: Sort these into 'a beat' or 'not a beat'.
items: a tap that drips once every second
a dog barking now and then
items.why: A beat repeats steadily with the same gap each time. One slam, or barks at odd times, do not repeat steadily.

items.p: Label the 8 beats of Adi talam in the picture: clap, little finger, ring finger, middle finger, clap, wave, clap, wave.
items.why: A strong answer puts the 8 hand shapes in order: a clap and three fingers, then clap and wave, then clap and wave.
items.art: Eight hand drawings in a circle with an empty label line under each.

items.p: Thenmozhi plays clap, clap, pat. Clap, clap, pat. Clap, clap, pat. How many claps does she make?
items.why: Each 'clap, clap, pat' has 2 claps. She plays it 3 times. 2 and 2 and 2 make 6.

items.p: Three friends explain why the big carton sounded lower than the matchbox.

views.says: Because it is bigger. Its big sides vibrate more slowly.
Because it is made of card, and card always sounds low.
Because it has much more air inside it, and that air vibrates too.

items.ask: Who do you agree with? Use what you found in the Big Box test. Then say whether another friend is partly right.
items.a: A strong answer agrees with Kavya and uses evidence: all the boxes were card, yet the small ones sounded high. So Farhan's reason cannot be right. Meena is partly right: the air inside a box vibrates too, and more air also makes a lower sound.
items.why: The matchbox and the carton were both card, so the material alone cannot explain it. Size changes both the sides and the amount of air inside.

items.p: Your little cousin Arjun says, 'Small boxes are broken drums, because they don't go boom.' What would you tell him?
items.a: Small boxes are not broken. They vibrate faster, so they make a high sound instead of a low one. A band needs high sounds too.
items.why: A strong answer explains that a small box's sides vibrate fast, which makes a high sound, and that high is just different from low.

items.p: Design one instrument that can play a high, a middle and a low sound. Draw it and label which part makes each sound.
items.a: For example, three boxes of different sizes taped in a row, labelled low for the biggest and high for the smallest. Or three bottles with different amounts of water.
items.why: A strong design uses different sizes, or different amounts of air, and labels the biggest or emptiest one as low.

items.p: A tabla has two drums, one small and one big. Which one gives the lower sounds?
items.why: The big drum, called the bayan, gives the deep, low sounds. The small drum, the dayan, gives the high ones. Bigger usually means lower.

items.p: In the Sleepy Song, Dancing Song test, why did we count each song twice?
items.a: Because one count can go wrong, for example if you pat on every other beat. If two counts are close, we can trust them.
items.why: A strong answer says that repeating a test checks for mistakes.

items.p: Put these in order from the slowest beat to the fastest: a running person's footsteps, a sleeping person's breathing, a walking person's footsteps.
items.why: Sleeping breaths come only every few seconds. Walking steps come about twice a second, and running steps come faster still.

items.p: Match each change to what it does to the sound.
items.why: Size and the amount of air change high and low. How hard you hit changes loud and soft. How fast you play changes the tempo.

items.p: True or false: only humans can move in time to a beat.
items.why: False. Snowball the cockatoo and Ronan the sea lion both moved in time to music. Scientists still argue about how many other animals can.

items.p: Sort these changes: does each one make the sound higher or lower?
items.why: Smaller things, and less air, vibrate faster and sound higher. Bigger things, and more air, vibrate more slowly and sound lower.

items.p: Which change does NOT make a sound higher or lower?
items.why: Tapping harder makes the sound louder, but not higher or lower. The other three change the size or the amount of air, so they change the pitch.

applications: Drum makers make bigger drums for deeper sounds. The tabla's big bayan gives the low sounds and the small dayan gives the high ones.
Temples hang big bells for deep sounds and small bells for high, bright sounds.
Speakers that play deep bass sounds are bigger than the small speakers that play high sounds.
Rowers in Kerala's snake boat races pull their oars in time to boat songs called vanchipattu, so the whole crew rows together.
Music teachers use a metronome, a machine that ticks a steady beat, to help students keep time.
People marching in a parade step on the same beat, so the whole group moves together.
Doctors listen to the beat of the heart, and count how fast it is, to check that a body is well.
Carnatic and Hindustani musicians keep the tala with their hands, so singers and drummers stay together.

open_questions.q: Why do humans enjoy rhythm, and want to move to a beat?
open_questions.why_open: Scientists have many ideas, for example that it helps groups work and stay together, or that it grew from the rocking of babies. Nobody knows for sure.

open_questions.q: Which other animals can feel a beat and move to it?
open_questions.why_open: Some parrots and one sea lion can. Scientists are still testing other animals, and argue about why some can and others seem not to.

open_questions.q: Why do people hear identical clock ticks as 'tick-tock'?
open_questions.why_open: Our minds group steady beats into twos or threes, even when every beat is the same. Scientists are still studying how the brain does this.

open_questions.q: Why did music begin at all?
open_questions.why_open: People have made music for a very long time: bone flutes found in Germany are more than 35,000 years old. But why people first made music is still argued about.

maths.problem: Thenmozhi's rhythm goes clap, clap, pat, clap, clap, pat, and keeps repeating. What is the 9th sound?
maths.explain: The pattern has 3 sounds: clap, clap, pat. So every 3rd sound is a pat: the 3rd, the 6th and the 9th. The 9th sound is a pat.
maths.context: This is about the Pattern Train game, where you lay sound cards in a line so that a pattern repeats.
maths.why_maths: Spotting the repeating part of a pattern lets you say what comes next without playing it all out.

maths.problem: One round of Adi talam has 8 beats. Paati counts 3 rounds. How many beats is that?
maths.explain: Each round is 8 beats. Three rounds is 8, 16, 24. So 3 groups of 8 is 24 beats.
maths.context: This is about the Ta Ka Di Mi activity, where you counted Adi talam with claps, fingers and waves.
maths.why_maths: Musicians count in rounds. Knowing how many beats are in a round lets you work out a whole song.

maths.problem: In the Sleepy Song, Dancing Song test, Bidisha counted 16 pats for the lullaby and 32 for the dance song, each in 15 seconds. How many more pats did the dance song have?
maths.answer: 16 more pats. The dance song had twice as many.
maths.explain: 32 take away 16 is 16. And 16 and 16 make 32, so the dance song's beat was twice as fast.
maths.context: This is about the Sleepy Song, Dancing Song test, where you counted pats for 15 seconds.
maths.why_maths: Comparing the two numbers tells us how much faster one tempo is, not only that it is faster.

maths.problem: In the eyes-shut round of the Big Box test, Kavya named 4 boxes right, Arjun named 2 and Appa named 3. Make a tally for each. Who named the most right?
maths.explain: Kavya: IIII, 4. Arjun: II, 2. Appa: III, 3. 4 is the biggest number, so Kavya named the most right.
maths.context: This is about the eyes-shut round of the Big Box test, where one person tapped a box and another named it from the sound alone.
maths.why_maths: A tally keeps count as you go, and makes it easy to compare who got more.

maths.problem: Mee-nak-shi is 3 claps. Ka-vya is 2 claps. Far-han is 2 claps. If you clap all three names, one after the other, how many claps is that?
maths.explain: 3 and 2 make 5. 5 and 2 make 7. So all three names make 7 claps.
maths.context: This is about Name Rhythms, where you clap one clap for each part of a name.
maths.why_maths: Adding up the claps tells you how long a rhythm will be before you play it.

roots.context: We have tapped big and small boxes, hooted bottles and kept a beat together. Now we ask what the Big Box test tells us about sound, and about ourselves.

deep_truth.truth: In the Big Box test, every box was card, tapped the same way. The big carton boomed low and the matchbox ticked high. The steel bowls did the same, from biggest to smallest. So one material can make a low note or a high note, and its size and shape decide which.
deep_truth.habit: We think each material has its own sound: card goes 'tok' and steel goes 'ting'. But the same card made a deep boom and a high tick. The size and shape of a thing change its note as well as what it is made of.
deep_truth.evidence: Every box was cardboard, and every tap was one finger on the middle of the top. Yet the big carton went 'dhum', the shoebox 'tok' and the matchbox 'tik'. Three steel bowls from one set rang lowest for the biggest and highest for the smallest.

three.who_am_i: Your voice comes from two small folds in your throat that vibrate. Grown-up men usually have longer folds, so their voices are usually lower.
three.what_is_life: Many living beings keep time with each other. Frogs call in turns at night, and a cockatoo called Snowball danced to the beat of songs.
three.what_is_this_world: The world is full of beats that come round again and again: day and night, your breath and your heartbeat.

roots.thread: A tap is one quick push. A box answers it with a note of its own, set by its size and shape. The same tap gave a big carton, a small box and a steel bowl three different notes. Everything is conscious, the box and the bowl too, and each answers in its own way. When many players follow one beat, all those different notes join into one song.

teachings.source: Zhuangzi, chapter 2 ('The Adjustment of Controversies', also called 'All Things Are Equal')
teachings.teaching: The Chinese thinker Zhuangzi describes the wind blowing through a great forest. The hollows in the trees are of every size and shape. When the wind blows, each hollow makes its own sound: some roar, some whistle, some hum.
teachings.link: Your bottle hooted when you blew across it, and hooted higher with less air inside. One breath made a different note in each different hollow.

teachings.source: Natya Shastra, chapter 28 in most editions
teachings.teaching: The Natya Shastra, an old Indian book on drama, music and dance, sorts instruments into four kinds: stringed ones (tata), drums covered with skin (avanaddha), solid ones that are struck (ghana), and hollow ones that are blown (sushira).
teachings.link: Your ektara is a tata instrument, and your bottle hooter is a sushira. Your box drum is a drum too, but its cover is card, not skin. In each kind, a different part vibrates: a string, a skin, a solid body or the air.

science.text: Every sound comes from something vibrating. For things of the same material and shape, bigger ones vibrate more slowly and make lower notes.
Some other animals, such as Snowball the cockatoo and Ronan the sea lion, can move in time to a beat. Scientists still argue about which animals can do it, and why.

other_view.view: Many physicists would say a box does not answer a tap at all. They say it simply vibrates in the way its size and shape allow, as a ball rolls down a slope, with no sensing involved.

playtest: Every experiment, activity, game, challenge and project was walked through as if at home today. The Big Box test needs boxes that are very different in size, because two boxes of nearly the same size sound almost alike: the step says so. Boxes are tapped on a hard floor, since a mattress or sofa deadens them. The steel-bowl check uses one stacking set, so the steel is the same and only the size changes, and the bowls stand on a towel so they do not slide. In the tempo test, children often pat on every word or on every other beat, so the steps say how to spot this and count again. The bottle hooter takes several tries, so a grown-up tries first, and the child may listen instead. A glass bottle stays on a towel on the floor. The tissue-box ektara needs a band long enough to go round the box the long way: two shorter bands looped together work. Pattern Train: a 3-part pattern does not fit exactly into 8 cards, and the parent note says this is a good thing to notice.

how_we_found_out.story: About 1,900 years ago, a Greek writer called Nicomachus told a story about Pythagoras. Pythagoras was walking past a blacksmith's shop and heard the hammers ringing. Some of them sounded sweet together. Nicomachus said Pythagoras weighed the hammers and found simple numbers: 12, 9, 8 and 6. So, said the story, the weight of a hammer sets its note, in neat steps. For more than 1,000 years, people copied this story into their books. Then, around 1589 in Italy, a lute player and music writer called Vincenzo Galilei decided to test it. He hung weights on strings, the way the story said. The numbers did not work. To make a string's note jump up by one big step, called an octave, doubling the weight was not enough. He needed four times the weight. Hammers do not follow the story's numbers either, because a hammer's note depends on its size and shape. Vincenzo had shown that a famous old story was wrong, simply by trying it. His son, Galileo Galilei, grew up to test many old ideas in the same way.
how_we_found_out.who: Nicomachus, a Greek writer who told the story about Pythagoras, and Vincenzo Galilei, an Italian lute player and music writer who tested it
how_we_found_out.when: About 100 CE (the story), and about 1589 (the test)
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: That the weight of a hammer, or of a weight hung on a string, sets its note in simple steps. When Vincenzo Galilei tried it, he needed four times the weight, not twice, to raise a string's note by an octave.
how_we_found_out.art: A lute player in an old Italian room hanging small weights on strings stretched along a wooden board, with an old book open beside him showing blacksmiths with hammers.
